abstract: Challenger, Gray & Christmas job cuts report for October 2026, released November 5, 2026. US employers announced 43,994 cuts, the lowest October total since 2023 and 71 percent below October 2025. The finding that matters for jobsdata.ai is a reversal in attribution: AI was cited in only 1,265 October cuts, its lowest month of the year, and Market/Economic Conditions has overtaken AI as the leading reason for cuts in 2026. AI had been the leading 2026 reason in every prior month of the year.
keyFindings: 'AI was cited for 1,265 cuts in October, its lowest monthly total this year.' That is down from 3,961 in September and from the spring and summer peaks.
'AI has been cited in 121,401 job cut announcements so far in 2026, approximately 20% of all cuts,' and in 193,226 since 2023, when Challenger began tracking AI as a distinct reason.

'With 130,531 cuts so far this year, Market/Economic Conditions has overtaken Artificial Intelligence (AI) as the leading reason for job cuts in 2026.' This is the first month of 2026 in which AI is not the top cited reason year to date.

October cuts were 43,994, up 2 percent from September's 43,281 but down 71 percent from 153,074 in October 2025, and the lowest October since 2023's 36,836. It was the eighth month this year below the same month a year earlier.
Year-to-date cuts were 617,189, down 44 percent from 1,099,500 in the first 10 months of 2025, and the lowest January-October total since 2022.

Technology announced 5,576 cuts in October, its lowest monthly total of the year, but still leads all industries with 171,501 year to date, 28 percent of all 2026 cuts, having already passed its full-year 2025 total of 154,445.

Hiring plans were 444,692 in October, up 57 percent year over year and the highest October since at least 2009, though Amazon's 300,000 seasonal hires account for nearly all of Technology's 300,252 announced hires - short-term seasonal work rather than permanent headcount.

Challenger's own reading: 'AI dominated layoff announcements through the spring and summer, but this fall companies are pointing to demand and economic conditions. That is a more cautious signal, though the overall pace of cutting remains low.'
methodology: Monthly tally of publicly announced US job cuts compiled from news reports, company statements and WARN notices, with a single primary reason attributed to each announcement from what the employer says publicly. Announcements are counted when announced, not when cuts take effect, and the reason taxonomy is Challenger's own.
qualifiers: Tier 2. Announced cuts are not realized separations: they may be phased, reduced, or offset by hiring elsewhere, and the series double-counts nothing but captures only cuts large or public enough to be reported. AI attribution reflects what employers choose to say, which is the series' central weakness in both directions - firms have incentives to credit AI for restructurings decided on other grounds, and incentives to avoid naming AI where it was the cause. The attribution shift this month is therefore at least as much a change in corporate framing as a change in cause, and Challenger says as much. Announced cuts are counts, not shares of employment, so this enters jobsdata.ai as an overlay. One month of a reason-ranking change is thin evidence for a turning point: AI's 121,401 and Market/Economic Conditions' 130,531 are close enough that the ranking could flip back.
